newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africans launch bid to ban "canned" lion hunts.
newsitem.headline: S.Africans launch bid to ban "canned" lion hunts.

text.p: South Africans are reverting to the "people's power" which ousted apartheid to moot a ban of staged lion hunts, where Africa's premier cats are bred for the bullet to cater for foreign trophy hunters.

Over 13,000 protests have been lodged with the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW), coordinating a campaign for a moratorium on all lion hunts and an official inquiry into staged hunts in under a week.

"We have never had such an overwhelming outpouring of horror and disgust," IFAW Africa director David Barritt told a news briefing in Johannesburg on Thursday. "But it is not enough just to be outraged. It's a big business.
"We call for an immediate moratorium on all lion hunting in South Africa and for an independent inquiry into the industry. We believe that unless this is done, it will continue."

American tourists alone are estimated to spend over $1 million a year on big game hunting in South Africa. Rare imported animals such as tigers and jaguars can be hunted illegally in South Africa for $100,000.

The practice has gained wide notoriety following an investigation initiated by IFAW Africa which led to the screening of a television programme depicting "canned", or staged hunts, on Britain's Cookes' Report and on South Africa's Carte Blanche investigative programme.

Hidden cameras showed how lions from the famed Kruger National Park were lured into a private game reserve, drugged and offered up as a sitting ducks in fenced off enclosures. One lioness filmed was gunned down in front of her three cubs.

"The image that many people have of lion hunting as a dangerous and brave pursuit in the wilderness has become a crass commercial industry that takes no cognisance of regulations or animal welfare," said Barritt.
The country's hospitality industry, represented by the 1,300-strong Fedhasa grouping, joined the protest campaign on Thursday vowing to weed out any of its members involved in the hunts.
"We will apply some peer pressure," Fedhasa executive director Deon Viljoen told reporters at the news briefing.
Interpol and the South African police's Endangered Species Protection Unit are investigating the reports.
But in many cases the hunts are legal under loopholes in existing laws and permits allowing year-round hunts on farms with game-proof fences if they are larger than 400 hectares. Permits are free.
South Africa's environmental minister Pallo Jordan said in a statement he condemned the canned hunts and pledged the authorities would act to stamp out inhumane hunting methods.
"Where necessary, legislative action will be instituted to tighten the regulation of hunting activities in the areas where illegal hunting activities have been reported," Jordan said.
Barritt, however, questioned the authorities' commitment to ending the canned hunts, and said he had first met Jordan a year ago to request action, without success.
"He made soothing noises...but nothing has happened. The minister of environmental affairs must be made to conduct an independent inquiry immediately."
